task_title: Compliance with Departure, En Route, and Arrival Procedures and Clearances
area: Area V. Air Traffic Control Clearances and Procedures
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe, at instructor depth, how a pilot selects current publications, splits responsibility with ATC on DPs, en route charts and STARs, picks frequencies and navaids, runs the right checklists, complies with vectors and restrictions, intercepts courses, handles a radio failure on a procedure and uses an MFD to watch track and drift, and you can teach each of these to an instrument learner and catch the common errors.
why: Pilot and controller responsibilities overlap on purpose so that one can make up for the other's failure [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]], but that only works if the pilot knows exactly which part is his. More than two-thirds of CFIT accidents come from an altitude error or a lack of vertical situational awareness, and 7.2 percent of them happen during the descent [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. A learner who flies every SID, airway and STAR by rote, without knowing what each clearance does and does not allow, is the pilot those numbers describe.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner, departing a nontowered airport in a G1000 Cessna 172, is "cleared to the destination airport as filed, climb and maintain 6,000." She plans to turn on course right after takeoff because "ATC has radar and will keep me clear of the hills." Which parts of that belief are wrong, where would she find what she must fly, and how would you get her to discover it herself instead of telling her?

key_terms.def: A preplanned IFR procedure that gives obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure; the two types are the ODP and the SID [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].
Obstruction clearance by the least onerous route; it may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].
An ATC procedure, always charted graphically, for obstruction clearance and transition to the en route structure; you need an ATC clearance before you fly it [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].
An ATC coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and links the en route structure to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a]].
Abbreviated clearances to fly the procedure's lateral path and meet its published altitude and speed restrictions [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h6]] [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]].
ATC lets you start the climb or descent when you wish, at any rate, with temporary level-offs; once you vacate an altitude you may not return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]].
A heading from ATC, given in controlled airspace for separation, noise abatement or an operational advantage, and in any class of airspace when the pilot asks [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]].
The point between two facilities where you change the receiver from the station behind to the station ahead; normally midway unless charted [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]].

Off-route obstruction clearance altitude: 1,000 ft of clearance, 2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas, not assessed for NAVAID signal, radar or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]].
The volume in which the FAA ensures a NAVAID signal is strong enough and free of interference; it is mainly for off-route navigation [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].
The difference between the displayed path and the aircraft's displayed position relative to it [[40:60|AC 90-105A C.7.4.5]].
The angle between heading, where the nose points, and track, the actual path over the ground [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].

chunks.title: Two people, one clearance: how pilot and controller share the job

body.p: **Pilot and controller responsibilities.** Pilot responsibilities are in the CFRs, and controller responsibilities are in FAA Order JO 7110.65 and supplemental directives [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]. The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the safe operation of the aircraft [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]. The controller's first priority is separating aircraft and issuing radar safety alerts [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]].

The two sets of duties overlap on purpose, so that if one party fails, the other can often make up for it [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]. The IPH says the same about departures: without the interest and attention of both ATC and the pilot, the IFR system cannot work [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]. The Instrument lessons IR.III.A and IR.V.B cover copying and flying these clearances; this lesson adds the instructor's view of who owns what.

head: Pilot
Controller
rows: Clearance
Acknowledges it, asks for clarification or an amendment when it is unclear or unsafe, complies promptly [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]]
Issues clearances that fit the operation, assigns altitudes at or above the minimum IFR altitudes, makes sure readbacks are correct [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]] [[34:3|AIM 5-5-2]]
Vectors
Complies promptly with assigned headings and altitudes and questions any that look wrong [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]
Vectors IFR aircraft at or above minimum vectoring altitudes, except in cases such as radar departures [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]
See and avoid
When weather permits, sees and avoids traffic, terrain and obstacles, whatever the flight plan [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]
Gives traffic information outside positive control airspace, workload permitting, and safety alerts [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]
Speed
Complies unless the speed is unsafe for the aircraft, may refuse excessive adjustments, holds ±10 knots [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]
Assigns speed adjustments when needed, not as a substitute for good vectoring [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.123: once you have a clearance, do not deviate unless you get an amended clearance, have an emergency, or are following a TCAS resolution advisory, and if you are unsure, ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. Do not fly contrary to an ATC instruction except in an emergency [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]. Tell ATC as soon as possible about an emergency or RA deviation [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]], and never follow a clearance or instruction meant for another aircraft [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]].

Application: draw two overlapping circles on the whiteboard, one for the pilot and one for ATC, and fill them in phase by phase as the lesson goes on. Each chunk below adds items to one of the circles, and the overlap is where the learner must watch the controller as much as the controller watches him.

check.q: Your learner says, "If ATC gave it to me, it must be safe." Which AIM principle do you use to correct him?
check.a: Responsibilities overlap on purpose so each side can catch the other's failure [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]. The pilot questions any heading or altitude he believes is wrong [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]] and asks for an amendment when a clearance is unacceptable for safety [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]].

chunks.title: Selecting current and appropriate navigation publications

body.p: **Selection and use of current and appropriate navigation publications.** Aeronautical information changes fast, so check the effective date on every chart and publication and discard obsolete ones [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. In the U.S., 0901Z is the changeover time for updated information, and NOTAMs carry the changes that come between chart cycles [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. Before an IFR flight the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information about it [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

Currency

Revised every 56 days [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]]

Revised every 56 days [[34:195|AIM 9-1-5]]
Area charts
Congested terminal areas at a larger scale; handy for finding a fix you have just been cleared to [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]] [[29:136|IPH 3-24]]
Included with the low chart sets [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]]
Terminal Procedures Publication
IAPs, DP and STAR charts, airport diagrams, and the takeoff minimums and (obstacle) DP section [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]] [[34:197|AIM 9-1-5]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]]
A Change Notice comes out midway between revisions [[34:196|AIM 9-1-5]]
Chart Supplement
Airports, NAVAIDs, communications, weather sources, preferred IFR routes, clearance delivery phone numbers [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]] [[29:68|IPH 2-8]] [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]]
Issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]

Every published RNAV procedure must be loaded from it by name [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]
Updated every 28 days [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]

body.p: **Checking the database.** Before flight, confirm the date and time of use is before the database expiration and that the provider has not limited a waypoint or procedure; in flight, check that waypoint names, order and layout match the chart [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]]. If an amended chart has been published for a procedure, or its amendment date is on or after the database expiration date, do not use the database for it [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. A database may not hold every procedure, because some manufacturers trim records to fit storage [[29:263|IPH 6-13]].

callout.text: The AIM is not consistent on expired databases. Its text says the onboard navigation data must be current [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]], while its GPS table notes allow IFR en route and terminal use of an expired database after the data is verified for correctness, and an approach with a current database or proof the procedure has not been amended [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]]. RNAV procedures must come from the current database [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]. Teach learners to fly with a current database. Hand-held and VFR GPS units are only an aid to situational awareness under IFR [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].

Application: make the learner the librarian. Before each IFR cross-country, have her lay out which chart, which TPP page and which Chart Supplement entry answers each phase of the flight, and read the effective dates aloud. It turns K1 from a memorized list into a habit.

check.q: Your learner says her tablet charts are fine because the app "updates itself." What do you have her check?
check.a: The effective date on each chart and publication, using current editions only, plus NOTAMs for changes between cycles [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]], and the GPS database date against the time of use [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

chunks.title: Departure procedures: who owns obstacle clearance, and when

body.p: **Pilot and controller responsibilities with regard to DPs.** An ODP gives obstacle clearance by the least onerous route and may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors; a SID needs a clearance before you fly it [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]. The Instrument lesson IR.V.B covers design criteria and climb gradients; here the focus is the split of responsibility you must teach.

head: Situation
Who provides obstacle clearance
rows: Part 91 IFR departure with no ODP filed or cleared, no SID and no DVA headings
The pilot [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]]
Flying the ODP, SID, VCOA or DVA headings as cleared

The procedure, as long as the pilot flies its path and climb; he still checks takeoff minimums and obstacle notes, and on a VCOA or DVA he stays clear of low, close-in obstacles himself [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9f]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f2]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f3]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f4]]
"Radar contact" on departure, no heading given
Still the pilot: radar contact does not relieve him of terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]] [[29:54|IPH 1-38]]
Radar vectors after takeoff
ATC, once it begins navigational guidance with vectors [[29:54|IPH 1-38]] [[29:58|IPH 1-42]]
Vectored off an ODP, or given an altitude below one on it
ATC; the ODP is canceled [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]

body.p: **The pilot's part.** Before an IFR departure the pilot considers the terrain and obstacles, finds out whether an ODP exists, decides whether obstacles can be avoided visually or the ODP must be flown, and thinks through degraded climb performance [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h1]]. At an airport with no published IAP, and so no DP, he decides what will assure a safe departure [[34:9|AIM 5-5-14]]. ATC assigns an ODP only when it is needed for separation, so finding it is the pilot's job, and if he flies an ODP that was not in his clearance he should tell ATC [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

**The controller's part.** At towered airports the controller specifies takeoff direction, a turn or an initial heading when needed, consistent with DPs or DVAs; without a tower but inside a Class E surface area, the controller gets the pilot's agreement that the procedure keeps him clear of terrain and obstructions [[34:9|AIM 5-5-14]]. When an initial heading takes the aircraft off an assigned procedure, the controller assigns an altitude with it, and ATC includes a DP in the clearance when compliance is needed for separation [[34:10|AIM 5-5-14]].

**SIDs.** To accept a SID the pilot needs the charted procedure, the climb performance, the navigation accuracy and an understanding of the whole SID [[29:46|IPH 1-30]]. Once he accepts it, ATC is responsible for traffic separation and expects the SID flown as charted, because its design considers obstacle clearance [[29:46|IPH 1-30]]. Vectored off a SID, he considers it canceled with its altitude and speed restrictions unless ATC says "expect to resume SID" [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. Crossing altitudes and speed restrictions on an ODP cannot be canceled or amended by ATC [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h9]].

A radar SID like this one usually starts with vectors right after takeoff and often has its own lost communication procedure, which the pilot is expected to fly, not necessarily the AIM procedure [[29:42|IPH 1-26]]. Mandatory notes on a DP, such as required equipment or radar, mean that if he cannot comply he must not file the procedure [[29:44|IPH 1-28]].

callout.text: Learners hear "radar contact" and relax. Have them say who is protecting them from terrain at each point of the climb: themselves until vectors start, the procedure when they fly it as published, and ATC once it vectors them [[29:54|IPH 1-38]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

check.q: Your learner asks why ATC never puts the ODP in his clearance from a nontowered field. What do you answer?
check.a: ATC assigns an ODP from a nontowered airport only when it is needed for aircraft separation [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9g]]. Finding the ODP is his job, and if he flies it without it being in his clearance he should tell ATC [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

chunks.title: En route low and high altitude charts: reading them as responsibilities

body.p: **Pilot and controller responsibilities with regard to En Route Low and High Altitude Charts.** Low altitude charts serve IFR navigation below 18,000 MSL and high altitude charts at and above FL 180 [[29:74|IPH 2-14]] [[29:77|IPH 2-17]]. Every altitude and line on them comes with a condition the pilot must meet.

head: Chart data
What the pilot must do with it
rows: Airway or direct course

Fly the centerline of an ATS route, or the direct course between the fixes of any other route, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]]; lead turns to stay within the airway [[33:381|AIM 5-3-5]]
MEA and MOCA

The MEA assures acceptable navigation signal coverage and obstacle clearance between the fixes; the MOCA meets obstacle clearance but assures VOR signal coverage only within 22 NM of the VOR [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. Stay at or above them; below the MEA down to the MOCA only with signals available and, navigating by VOR, within 22 NM of that VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]]
MRA
The lowest altitude at which the fix can be identified when that is higher than the MEA; below it he may not receive the off-route NAVAID that defines the fix [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
MAA
The highest altitude on the route at which adequate reception of navigation signals is assured; plan to stay at or below it [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
MCA and MTA
Cross the fix at or above the MCA when climbing to a higher MEA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]]; be at or above an MTA by the turn point [[33:381|AIM 5-3-7]]
Changeover point
Change NAVAIDs there, or midway if none is charted [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]]
Unusable segment
Do not file or accept a clearance that navigates on it [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]]
OROCA
Awareness, planning and contingency use only [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]]; not an acceptable altitude for random RNAV direct flights [[29:87|IPH 2-27]]
Reporting points
Solid triangles are compulsory, open triangles only on request; stop routine reports in radar contact [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]]

body.p: **The controller's side.** ATC assigns IFR altitudes at or above the minimum IFR altitudes in controlled airspace [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]]. When delay is expected at a clearance limit other than the destination, ATC issues complete holding instructions unless the pattern is charted, plus an EFC [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]]. Unpublished RNAV routes need ATC radar monitoring, except for GNSS aircraft cleared via filed published waypoints from the database [[33:379|AIM 5-3-4]]. Off airways, the pilot owns obstruction clearance on direct segments outside controlled airspace, where chart MEAs may not apply [[29:83|IPH 2-23]].

**Reports the pilot owes.** Under IFR in controlled airspace the pilot keeps a continuous watch on the right frequency and reports, as soon as possible, the time and altitude passing each designated reporting point (in radar contact, only the ones ATC asks for), any unforecast weather, and anything else that affects safety of flight [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]]. He reports in-flight malfunctions of navigation, approach or communication equipment as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. Without being asked, he also tells ATC when he vacates an assigned altitude, cannot climb or descend at 500 fpm or more, misses an approach, changes cruise TAS by 5 percent or 10 knots, reaches or leaves a holding fix or clearance limit, and, when not in radar contact, leaves the FAF inbound or finds an estimate off by more than 2 minutes [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]] [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

rows: Altitudes
At or above 18,000 MSL [[34:195|AIM 9-1-5]]
Routes
Victor airways in black, T-routes in blue [[33:378|AIM 5-3-4]] [[33:379|AIM 5-3-4]]

callout.text: Application: hand the learner a highlighter and a low chart and have him trace the route, circling every MEA change, MCA flag, COP and unusable segment, and saying what each requires of him. That ties chart symbols to actions, the correlation level the AIH calls the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

check.q: Off airways below 18,000, your learner plans a GPS direct leg at the OROCA. What do you tell him?
check.a: OROCAs are for awareness, planning and contingencies and are not assessed for signal, radar or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]]. The IPH says they are not an acceptable altitude for random RNAV direct flights [[29:87|IPH 2-27]].

chunks.title: STARs: what the arrival clearance does and does not allow

body.p: **Pilot and controller responsibilities with regard to STARs.** ATC may issue a STAR whenever it sees fit, even if the pilot did not ask for one [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1b]] [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]. Using one requires at least the approved chart, and RNAV STARs must be retrievable by name from the database [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]]. Accepting or refusing it is the pilot's call; write "NO STAR" in the remarks if you do not want them [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]].

head: Item on or about the STAR
Is it binding?
rows: Published speed restriction
Yes, unless ATC modifies it [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]]
Last published speed at the end of the STAR
Yes: keep it until ATC deletes it, assigns a new speed, vectors you, clears you direct or clears you for the approach [[33:282|AIM 4-4-12a]]
"Expect" altitude or speed
No: planning only until ATC issues it, and not used in lost comm unless ATC said to expect it [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]]
MEA printed on the STAR
Not a restriction, but stay above it unless ATC clears you lower [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
Your last assigned altitude
Yes: keep it until ATC authorizes descent, for example with "descend via" [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
A vector or clearance off the STAR
Cancels the STAR and its restrictions; ATC gives an altitude and, if needed, a speed [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]

body.p: **The controller's side.** ATC must ensure obstacle clearance when it issues "descend via", and assigns a crossing altitude at the joining fix when none is published for an aircraft cleared direct to the STAR [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. If ATC intends to clear the aircraft back onto the STAR, it tells the pilot where to expect to resume [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. On each new frequency under "descend via", the pilot reports the altitude leaving, "descending via" and the procedure name, the runway transition if assigned, and any restrictions not on the chart [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

The STAR legend separates mandatory, minimum and maximum altitudes and airspeeds, shows MEAs, MOCAs and MAAs, and even has symbols for a lost communications track and holding pattern [[2:130|Chart Users' Guide p 130]].

**PBN STARs.** Public PBN STARs are normally RNAV 1, RNP 1 or A-RNP, and everything listed in the chart's PBN box is required [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1e]]. RNAV 1 and RNP 1 both mean a total system error of not more than 1 NM for 95 percent of the flight time [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1e]]; an RNP specification adds onboard performance monitoring and alerting, an RNAV specification does not [[40:14|AC 90-105A 4.1.1.3]]. On RNAV 1 DPs and STARs the pilot must use a CDI, flight director and/or autopilot in lateral navigation mode [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]].

callout.text: Application: an unexpected STAR lowers situational awareness until the pilot has studied it [[23:337|IFH 11-12]]. Practice that on the ground: hand the learner a STAR he has never seen, give him two minutes, then ask what his clearance lets him do laterally, vertically and with speed.

check.q: Descending via a STAR, your learner is told, "Turn left heading 270, maintain 11,000." What happens to the STAR's altitude and speed restrictions?
check.a: Vectored off a STAR, he considers it canceled with its altitude and speed restrictions; ATC gives an altitude and, if needed, a speed, and says where to expect to resume if it plans to [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

chunks.title: Selecting and using the right frequency, phase by phase

body.p: **Selection and use of appropriate communications frequencies.** Controller frequencies are on departure, approach and airport charts and in the Chart Supplement [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]. Weather frequencies such as ATIS, AWOS and ASOS are on approach charts too [[29:26|IPH 1-10]].

head: Phase
Where the frequency comes from
What to teach
rows: Clearance at a towered airport
Clearance delivery or ground; pre-taxi clearance programs are listed in the Chart Supplement [[33:343|AIM 5-2-1]]
Under a pre-taxi program, call not more than 10 minutes before proposed taxi time [[33:343|AIM 5-2-1]]
Clearance at a nontowered airport
Chart Supplement frequency or telephone number [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]], an RCO or a GCO [[29:60|IPH 1-44]]
Say it is IFR and give departure and destination on first contact [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]]
Departure
Given before takeoff, or left out if it is printed on an assigned DP [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]]
Do not switch until told [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]]; give the altitude on first contact [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b]] [[29:54|IPH 1-38]]
Center
Sector frequencies on en route charts and in the Chart Supplement [[29:66|IPH 2-6]] [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]
Expect the same controller on different remote site frequencies [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]
Flight Service
RCO frequencies over NAVAID and communication boxes on en route charts [[2:65|Chart Users' Guide p 65]]
Weather and flight plan business go to Flight Service, not Center [[33:359|AIM 5-3-1a]]
Approach
ARTCC tells you to contact approach before the destination radio facility [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3a]]
Get airport and weather information as early as practical [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]

body.p: On en route charts, ARTCC remote sites appear as serrated boxes with the Center name, sector or site name and frequencies [[23:29|IFH 1-10]] [[2:67|Chart Users' Guide p 67]]. If flights may be out of range, those boxes help find the nearest Center frequency [[29:66|IPH 2-6]] [[29:67|IPH 2-7]].

**Using them.** A frequency change normally reads "contact (facility) (frequency) at (time, fix or altitude)", and the pilot keeps listening on the old frequency until that point [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b]]. In radar contact, give the assigned altitude with "level", "climbing to" or "descending to", plus the altitude you are leaving [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b]]. If a Center frequency seems dead, wait at least 1 minute, then try the transferring controller, another Center frequency or Flight Service [[29:108|IPH 2-48]]. If ATC assigns a frequency the radio cannot select, ask for another [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

callout.text: Application: teach the second radio as a tool. Listening to ATIS on one receiver while working ATC on the other, and checking a NAVAID's identifier, are the reasons the IFH gives for using the audio switch panel [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]. Have the learner preset the next frequency before every handoff and say it aloud.

check.q: Center assigns your learner a frequency his older radio cannot tune. What should he do?
check.a: Ask for an alternative frequency. The IFH notes that radios with 25 kHz spacing are needed to get the full benefit of the ATC system [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

body.p: **Selection and identification of the navigation aids.** Choose NAVAIDs that are usable where you need them. The standard service volume is where the FAA ensures adequate signal strength free of interference; it is mainly for off-route navigation, while published routes and procedures may use NAVAIDs beyond it when an extended service volume is approved [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]]. Service volume restrictions are published first in NOTAMs, then in the Chart Supplement [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].

head: SSV class
Altitudes
Distance (NM)
rows: (T) Terminal
25 [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]
(L) Low
40 [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]
(H) High
40; 100; 130 [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]
(VL) VOR Low
40; 70 [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]

body.p: Altitudes are above the station's site elevation, and there is no coverage in a cone directly above the facility [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]. For direct routes off airways below 18,000 MSL, the IPH says to use NAVAIDs not more than 80 NM apart [[29:82|IPH 2-22]].

**Identification.** The only positive way to identify a VOR is its Morse code or its recorded voice identification [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]], and the pilot should listen to it before relying on the instrument [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. A missing identifier, or a T-E-S-T code, means the facility is off the air for maintenance and may be unreliable even with a signal; do not fly a procedure that is NOTAMed out of service even if the identifier is heard [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. An ADF has no warning flag, so the pilot should monitor an NDB's identification continuously [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]].

**Intersections, checks and substitutes.** Arrows next to an intersection show which NAVAID identifies it, and a hollow arrowhead means DME may be used [[23:29|IFH 1-10]]. To fly IFR on VORs, the equipment must be maintained under an approved procedure or operationally checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]: ±4° with a VOT or surface checkpoint, ±6° with an airborne checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] or the in-flight airway check [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]], or 4° between dual VORs [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]], logged with date, place and bearing error [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. A suitable RNAV system may substitute for an out-of-service VOR, DME or NDB, and the pilot may need to tell ATC [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].

callout.text: Careless tuning and identification is the first VOR operational error the IFH lists [[23:257|IFH 9-14]], and homing or tracking to the wrong station is a listed ADF error [[23:251|IFH 9-8]]. Require the identifier aloud every time a NAV frequency changes.

check.q: How does your learner find out whether a VOR on his route has a service volume restriction?
check.a: Restrictions are published first in NOTAMs and then with the NAVAID's listing in the Chart Supplement [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].

body.p: **Accomplishment of the appropriate checklist items.** The PTS evaluates checklist use throughout the practical test, and it accepts a review of the checklist after the elements are done when using it during the task would be unsafe or impracticable in a single-pilot airplane. For this Task, the checklists are the POH ones plus the IFR flows the handbooks describe.

head: Phase
Checklist or flow items in the sources
rows: Before taxi
ATIS copied, clearance copied and read back, DP reviewed, frequencies tuned and navigation equipment set for the departure [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]
Before takeoff
Before-takeoff checklist and run-up; on the runway, heading indicator agrees with the compass, transponder in ALT, lights and pitot heat on [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]
RNAV or RNP departure or arrival

Procedure loaded by name from the current database and matching the chart [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]; for RNP 1, confirm the correct procedure, waypoint sequence and constraints, and the correct sensor [[40:61|AC 90-105A C.7.5]] [[40:62|AC 90-105A C.7.5]]; after a runway or transition change, verify the change is loaded [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]]
Cruise and descent
POH cruise and descent checklists and descent data, reviewed before departure [[29:120|IPH 3-8]]
Arrival
Airport and weather information early, STAR reviewed, approach chart studied, fuel checked, landing checklists done early [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]

callout.text: Transponder timing differs by source. The current AIM says to select the altitude reporting mode and enable ADS-B during taxi-out, on any part of the movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]]. The 2012 IFH (FAA-H-8083-15B) still says to leave it on standby until takeoff clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. Teach the AIM.

body.p: Programming is a checklist item too. The PHAK lists checking everything programmed while on the ground and confirming the routing matches the planned route before departure as ways to keep situational awareness [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

callout.text: Application: teach flows tied to triggers, such as "new frequency, then identify" and "new clearance, then reprogram, then verify", and have the learner confirm each flow with the written checklist when workload allows. Ask him to say the trigger aloud; it shows you whether the flow is a habit or a guess.

check.q: Approach changes your learner's runway, and with it his RNAV STAR transition, during the descent. Which checklist item matters most?
check.a: Verify the new runway and transition are loaded and available for navigation [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]], and check that the waypoints are in the correct order and match the chart before using them [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].

chunks.title: Complying with vectors and assigned altitudes

body.p: **Pilot's responsibility for compliance with vectors and altitude restrictions.** When ATC assigns a heading, start the turn promptly, complete it, and hold the new heading until told otherwise [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10b]]. Accepting radar vectors does not relieve the pilot of responsibility for the flight: he keeps a safe altitude, tracks his position, and questions the controller or asks for an amended clearance when safety is in doubt [[29:67|IPH 2-7]]. When a vector takes him off a nonradar route, ATC says what the vector is for [[33:380|AIM 5-3-4c]].

On departure, "fly runway heading" means the published heading of the extended centerline with no drift correction [[29:58|IPH 1-42]]. The IFH notes that a Center clearance "leaving (altitude) fly (heading) or proceed direct when able" keeps terrain and obstruction clearance in the flight deck until the aircraft is above the minimum IFR altitude [[23:61|IFH 2-10]].

**Assigned altitudes.** In controlled airspace, cruise at the altitude ATC assigned [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]]. With no "pilot's discretion" and no restriction, start the climb or descent promptly at an optimum rate to 1,000 ft from the altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm, and tell ATC if you cannot do at least 500 fpm or must level off [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]]. A "cruise" clearance assigns a block from the minimum IFR altitude up to the cruise altitude; once you report leaving an altitude in it, you may not return without another clearance [[29:103|IPH 2-43]].

head: Clearance wording
What the pilot does
rows: "Descend and maintain 6,000."
Start down on receipt and use the suggested rates [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10e]]
"Descend at pilot's discretion, maintain 6,000."
Start when he wishes, any rate, level off as he likes, but no return to a vacated altitude [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]]
"Cross Lakeview VOR at or above FL 200, descend and maintain 6,000."
Pilot's discretion until Lakeview while meeting the restriction, then the suggested rates [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10e]]
"Expedite climb."
About best rate without unusual handling; canceled if the altitude is restated without "expedite" [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10i]]

callout.text: The last clearance has precedence. If ATC changes or restates the altitude to maintain and leaves out earlier altitude restrictions, those restrictions are canceled, including DP and STAR altitude restrictions [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]] [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10g]]. Published SID speed restrictions and the lateral path still apply unless ATC cancels them [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9h8]] [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h8]]. Learners who keep flying an old crossing restriction, or drop one ATC restated, need this rule drilled.

check.q: On a vector at 3,000 ft toward rising terrain, your learner sees a 2,900 ft ridge ahead on the terrain page. ATC is busy. What does the IPH expect of him?
check.a: Vectors do not relieve him of responsibility for safety; he keeps track of position and altitude and questions the controller or asks for an amended clearance if safety is in doubt [[29:67|IPH 2-7]]. The AIM also has the pilot question any heading or altitude he believes is wrong [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]].

chunks.title: Airspeed, climb and descent, and airspace restrictions

body.p: **Airspeed restrictions.** Comply with ATC speed adjustments unless the airplane's minimum or maximum safe airspeed conflicts, then advise ATC; the pilot may refuse adjustments that are excessive or contrary to the aircraft's operating specifications [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]. Hold an assigned speed within ±10 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12c]]. If the airplane cannot maintain an assigned airspeed, the pilot must advise ATC [[29:132|IPH 3-20]]. Report a cruise TAS change of 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

The 91.117 limits still apply under speed adjustments [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12e]]: 250 knots below 10,000 MSL, 200 knots at or below 2,500 ft AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport, and 200 knots under a Class B area [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117]]. Published speed restrictions on a SID or STAR are mandatory unless ATC changes them, and they apply independent of a climb via or descend via clearance [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]] [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]] [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. When ATC joins a speed and a descent with the word "then", the order given is the order of execution [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12e]].

**Climb and descent restrictions.** A crossing restriction lets the pilot choose how to descend only for the part of the flight it covers, and crossing at that altitude is a provision of the clearance [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10e]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10e]]. When climbing to a higher MEA, start right after the fix, but cross it at or above any MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]]. A climb gradient on a DP in the clearance is mandatory unless higher takeoff minimums are offered and the weather allows them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]].

**Airspace restrictions.** No one may fly in a restricted area contrary to its restrictions, or in a prohibited area, without permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]]. Class A needs an IFR clearance before entering [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]], and VFR-on-top is not permitted there [[34:9|AIM 5-5-13]]. Check NOTAMs for TFRs during planning [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]]. Plan random RNAV routes at least 3 NM from prohibited or restricted airspace [[29:88|IPH 2-28]], and file around SUA and ATCAAs scheduled to be active [[29:67|IPH 2-7]].

callout.text: Application: give the learner one realistic restriction per leg, such as "cross the VOR at or above 4,000" or "maintain 100 knots until the outer fix", and have him say his plan to meet it before he touches anything. ATC expects pilots to start slowing the minimum distance needed to cross a fix at a published speed [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]], so early planning is part of compliance.

check.q: Approach assigns your learner 160 knots in a trainer that cruises at 115. What should he say, and why?
check.a: "Unable." He must advise ATC when he cannot maintain an assigned airspeed [[29:132|IPH 3-20]], and it is his prerogative to refuse speed adjustments contrary to the aircraft's operating specifications [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]].

body.p: **Pilot's responsibility for the interception of courses, radials, and bearings.** Unless ATC authorizes otherwise, in controlled airspace the pilot flies the centerline of an ATS route, or the direct course between the fixes of any other route [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]]. Airways based on VORs are defined by the outbound radial, and LF/MF airways by the inbound bearing [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. To get established on a Victor airway, fly directly to a nearby VOR or intercept an airway radial along the route [[29:78|IPH 2-18]].

head: IFH course interception step
In Figure 9-16
rows: 1. Find the difference between the radial to intercept and the radial you are on
2. Double it for the intercept angle, not less than 20° nor more than 90°
3. Set the OBS to the desired radial or inbound course and turn to the intercept heading
4. Hold the heading until the CDI centers, leading the turn to avoid overshooting, then track

body.p: With an ADF, the rule of thumb is to double the relative bearing for the intercept angle and hold the heading until the needle deflects the same number of degrees to the other side [[23:251|IFH 9-8]]. In RNAV, an aircraft is established on course when it is within 1 times the required accuracy for the segment, for example within 2 NM on an RNAV 2 Q-route [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]].

**When ATC sets up the intercept.** On a vector to final, the pilot is not expected to turn inbound unless he has an approach clearance, and he should query the controller if crossing the final approach course is imminent and he has not been told [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b]]. Cleared for an approach while on an unpublished route or vectored, he keeps the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[34:4|AIM 5-5-4]].

callout.text: Intercept errors to teach by name: careless tuning and identification, turning the wrong way during orientation, not checking TO/FROM and getting reverse sensing, not paralleling the desired radial first, overshooting and undershooting, and chasing the CDI [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

check.q: Your learner is told, "Intercept Victor 25, resume own navigation." Which radial defines the airway, and what must he fly once on it?
check.a: Victor airways are defined by the outbound radial from the VOR [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. Once established he flies the airway centerline unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]].

chunks.title: Two-way radio failure where the procedures meet the rule

body.p: **Procedures to be used in the event of two-way communications failure.** The full rule and its timing are taught in FII.IX.A; here is how it ties into the procedures of this Task. In VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. In IFR conditions, fly the assigned route, the direct route to the fix in a vector clearance, the expected route, or the filed route, in that order [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]], at the highest of the assigned, minimum IFR and expected altitudes for the segment [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

head: Procedure
Lost comm link
rows: Radar SID
Often has its own lost communication procedure, which you are expected to fly, not necessarily the AIM procedure [[29:42|IPH 1-26]]
Vectored departure or en route
Direct from the point of failure to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(ii)]]
STAR "expect" altitudes and speeds
Not used in lost comm unless ATC said to expect them as part of a further clearance [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]]
STAR that ends in vectors
Look for a charted route from the STAR end to the IAF; if none, have a plan for that leg [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]
Center frequency silent
Wait at least 1 minute before deciding the frequency failed [[29:108|IPH 2-48]]

callout.text: Application: in the ground brief of every DP and STAR, ask "radio fails right here: what route, what altitude?" The STAR legend has a lost communications track symbol [[2:130|Chart Users' Guide p 130]], and the Denver radar SID prints its own lost communications procedure [[29:44|IPH Figure 1-25]].

check.q: Vectored for spacing on a STAR in IMC, your learner loses both radios. Which route does 91.185 give him?
check.a: The direct route from the point of failure to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(ii)]], at the highest of the assigned, minimum IFR and expected altitudes [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]].

chunks.title: MFDs and graphical displays: track, drift and the big picture

body.p: **The uses of the multifunction display and other graphical navigational displays.** An MFD can show a moving map, approach charts, terrain awareness and weather [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. Moving maps improve situational awareness by picturing the aircraft relative to NAVAIDs, waypoints, airspace, terrain and hazardous weather [[23:29|IFH 1-10]] [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]. RNAV equipment computes position, actual track and groundspeed, and shows distance, cross-track error and time estimates [[23:265|IFH 9-22]].

**Position track and wind drift.** Heading is where the nose points, track is the actual path over the ground, and the angle between them is the drift angle; correcting into the wind makes the track match the desired course [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. A display that shows desired track (DTK) next to actual track (TRK), as in the IPH reroute example, shows at a glance whether the wind correction is holding the course [[29:88|IPH Figure 2-48]]; comparing TRK with the heading shows the drift angle [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. On RNP 1 procedures, cross-track error should normally stay within half the RNP value, 0.5 NM [[40:61|AC 90-105A C.7.4.5]].

**Setting up the display.** The PHAK suggests choosing a map orientation (north up, track up, desired track up or heading up), setting map scale for en route or terminal work, using the terrain page at night or in IMC near mountains, and the nearest airports inset over inhospitable terrain [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. During RNP 1 operations the pilot must use a navigation map or textual display, plus a lateral deviation indicator, flight director or autopilot in LNAV [[40:60|AC 90-105A C.7.4.1]] [[40:60|AC 90-105A C.7.4.3]].

head: Limit
What to teach
rows: Not a primary source

AFMs prohibit using the moving map, terrain, traffic and datalink weather displays as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]], and the moving map is not a substitute for a low altitude en route chart [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]
The magenta line
A straight GPS course can run through high terrain or prohibited airspace, and the display can fail [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Traffic
Not all traffic is displayed, and the display aids, but does not replace, see and avoid [[23:337|IFH 11-12]]
Datalink weather
NEXRAD is 5 to 15 minutes or more old; use it only for strategic avoidance [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]
Vectored off an RNP procedure
Do not change the flight plan until cleared to rejoin or given a new route [[40:61|AC 90-105A C.7.4.7]], and avoid deleting waypoints early [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]]

callout.text: Application: use the MFD as a cross-check, not the answer. Have the learner predict the track and the time to the next fix before he looks, then compare. The PHAK recommends double-checking the system, verbal callouts even when single-pilot, and backing up GPS with VOR [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

check.q: On a busy terminal arrival, your learner's MFD is north up at a wide en route scale, and he keeps losing the next fix. What do you suggest?
check.a: Manage the display for the task: the PHAK suggests choosing the map orientation (north, track, desired track or heading up) and setting the map scale for terminal work [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

chunks.title: Risk: how compliant pilots still end up in the wrong place

body.p: The basic causes of CFIT include poor situational awareness: a lack of vertical or horizontal position awareness relative to the ground, water or obstacles [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. CFIT accidents most often occur in reduced visibility with IMC, darkness or both [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. These are the hazards hidden inside routine compliance.

bullets: **Readback and hearback.** In an IPH example a pilot heard "leaving" instead of "reaching" 5,000 and climbed to 5,300 before Center caught it, with traffic a mile ahead at 6,000; the two words sound alike in the flight deck [[29:109|IPH 2-49]]. Read back altitudes, restrictions and vectors in the order given, with the call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]].

**Assuming ATC has the terrain.** Hearing "radar contact" does not relieve the pilot of terrain clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. Accepting a clearance below the MEA, MIA, MVA or OROCA makes the pilot responsible for terrain and obstruction clearance until he reaches it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]].

**Automation complacency.** Humans are poor monitors of automated systems, and the more reliable the system, the poorer the monitoring [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. In one study, crews with electronic displays went heads-down to solve close crossing restrictions on the FMS [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].
**Unexpected changes.** Distractions, unexpected events, complacency, high workload, unfamiliar situations and inoperative equipment all reduce situational awareness [[23:337|IFH 11-12]].

callout.text: Know the clearance, know the floor, know who has the terrain.

Application: when a learner is reactive, stop and have him reassess. The IFH says to regain situational awareness by reassessing the situation and seeking information from other sources, such as the navigation instruments or ATC [[23:337|IFH 11-12]].

check.q: Your learner reads back "leaving five thousand" when the clearance was "reaching five thousand", and the controller misses it. What does the IPH example teach?
check.a: That a readback is only a check if someone listens: the IPH crew's readback with "leaving" did not catch the difference, and they climbed through their altitude toward traffic [[29:109|IPH 2-49]]. Readbacks of the numbers are a double check between pilot and controller [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

chunks.title: Teaching this Task, and how the examiner tests it

body.p: **How it is tested.** The PTS objective is to describe each element from an instructional standpoint, and the Area V note has the evaluator select at least one Task. When you add an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor airplane certificate, the PTS table makes Area V required. The PTS also has the evaluator build scenarios that combine Tasks to judge risk management, so expect this Task inside a flight or oral scenario, not only as a recital.

**Teaching method.** Aim for the correlation level, where the learner ties each element to the others [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Scenario-based training fits this Task: realistic situations with more than one acceptable answer, which you have thought through in advance and in which the learner can make good and poor decisions without risk to safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

head: Common learner error
What you see
Fix
rows: Thinks "as filed" covers the hills
Turns on course at 400 ft from a field with an ODP
Brief who owns obstacle clearance; find the ODP in the TPP [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]] [[29:39|IPH 1-23]]
Descends on a STAR without a descent clearance
Starts down to an "expect" altitude
Last assigned altitude until descent is authorized [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
Keeps an old restriction, or drops a restated one
Levels at a canceled crossing altitude
The last clearance has precedence [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]]
Uses an unidentified NAVAID
CDI alive, no Morse code heard
Identify before use [[23:254|IFH 9-11]] [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]
Switches frequency early or misses the handoff point
Calls departure on the takeoff roll
Wait for the instruction, time, fix or altitude [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]] [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b]]
Flies the magenta line only
Cannot name the next fix, MEA or nearest airport
Predict before looking; back up GPS with VOR [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Old or wrong publication
Briefs from last cycle's chart
Check effective dates and NOTAMs [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]

callout.text: Application: build one IFR cross-country lesson that touches all nine elements: a publications check, an ODP or SID brief, frequency and NAVAID setup, checklists, a vector, a crossing restriction, an intercept, a radio failure briefed on the ground, and MFD cross-checks. In the airplane keep the lost comm part a discussion; in a training device you can play it out.

While the learner is under the hood, the traffic scan is yours. When weather permits, the pilot must see and avoid traffic, terrain and obstacles whatever the flight plan [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]], so don't let the clearance work pull your eyes inside.

check.q: The examiner asks how you would teach K6 to a learner who already flies vectors well. What do you add?
check.a: Move him from rote compliance to correlation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]: give scenarios where a vector, a restated altitude or a speed conflicts with the terrain or the airplane, and have him decide what to say, using the AIM rules on questioning headings [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]] and refusing excessive speeds [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]].

f7.caption: Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) chart legend. (Chart Users' Guide p 130)
f7.alt: The legend for STAR charts. Radio aids: compulsory and non-compulsory VOR, VORTAC, DME, TACAN and NDB symbols, a compass locator, localizer courses and a NAVAID box with notes that (T) shows a frequency protection range and an underline means no voice on the frequency. Routes: MAA, MEA and asterisked MOCA, an arrival route arrow with course and mileage, a transition route, a radial line, a dotted lost communications track, airway and jet route boxes, a holding pattern and a dotted lost comm holding pattern. Fixes: compulsory and non-compulsory reporting points and waypoints, flyover points and a computer navigation fix. Altitudes: mandatory (cross at), minimum (cross at or above), maximum (cross at or below) and block altitudes. Indicated airspeeds: mandatory, minimum and maximum. Special use airspace and airport symbols. Miscellaneous: changeover point, ADIZ, a true north arrow and terminus identifier boxes.

scenario.title: Out of the valley under a low deck
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII flying with an instrument learner in a Cessna 172 with a G1000. The trip is from a nontowered airport in a valley, which has a published ODP, to a towered airport 140 NM away that is served by an RNAV STAR. The ceiling is 900 overcast with tops near 6,000, and the learner has filed for 8,000 ft on a Victor airway with an MEA of 7,000. This is his first IFR cross-country in actual conditions.

questions.q: On the ground he says, "The clearance will cover everything." Which publications do you have him open, and why?
questions.a: The TPP takeoff minimums and (obstacle) DP section for his runway, because the ODP is his to find and fly [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]] [[29:39|IPH 1-23]]; the Chart Supplement for the clearance frequency or phone number [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]]; the low chart for MEAs, MCAs and COPs [[34:194|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]] [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]]; and the STAR chart, which he must have to accept the STAR [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]]. All with current dates and NOTAMs checked [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]].

questions.q: His clearance: "Cleared to the destination airport as filed, climb and maintain 8,000, clearance void if not off by 1430Z." Who provides obstacle clearance on the climb, and what does the void time mean for him?
questions.a: No DP was assigned, so obstacle clearance is his; he flies the ODP and tells ATC [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]] [[29:39|IPH 1-23]]. If he is not airborne by the void time he must advise ATC of his intentions as soon as possible, within the time ATC gives, never more than 30 minutes [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

questions.q: Climbing through 3,000 in cloud, Center says "radar contact" and nothing else. He turns direct to his first fix on the GPS. What do you say?
questions.a: Radar contact does not relieve him of terrain clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]]. Until ATC vectors him he keeps flying the ODP's path and at least the required climb toward the minimum en route altitude [[29:54|IPH 1-38]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f5]].

questions.q: En route, the VOR on his airway is NOTAMed out of service, but he hears an identifier and the needle looks fine. He wants to use it. What do you teach, and what are his options?
questions.a: Do not fly a procedure based on a NAVAID NOTAMed out of service even if the identifier is heard [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]], and disregard indications from a transmitter identified as unusable [[33:68|AIM 1-1-1]]. A suitable IFR RNAV system may substitute for the out-of-service VOR, and he may need to tell ATC [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].

questions.q: Approach clears him "direct the first fix, descend via the arrival." He loads it, but an old leg is still in the flight plan and the magenta line points the wrong way. How do you handle it as an instructor?
questions.a: If it is safe, let him find it, since a learner can be allowed poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Then have him compare the flight plan with the chart: RNAV procedures must be loaded by name and match the chart [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]], and the waypoint order must agree [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]]. Debrief verification as a habit [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

questions.q: In the brief before the descent he asks what he would do if the radios failed on the STAR. What do you want him to plan?
questions.a: Fly the cleared route at the highest of the assigned, minimum IFR and expected altitudes [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. STAR "expect" altitudes do not count unless ATC told him to expect them as part of a further clearance [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]], and if the STAR ends in vectors with no charted route to the IAF, he needs a plan for that leg [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

skills.do: Brief a DP, an en route segment and a STAR to a learner aloud, saying at each point what the pilot must do and what ATC provides: who has obstacle clearance, what each clearance authorizes, and which chart numbers are binding.
skills.practice: Pick a real departure, route and arrival near your home airport and give the brief to another applicant in under ten minutes, then have them quiz you with the AIM example clearances [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]] [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]] and the DP responsibilities [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h1]].

skills.do: Talk a learner through intercepting a radial and an airway on a moving map display: orientation, intercept angle, the lead, and checking track against desired track.
skills.practice: Fly the IFH interception steps in a training device while explaining each one aloud [[23:257|IFH 9-14]], then repeat using the display's DTK and TRK readouts [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]] [[29:88|IPH Figure 2-48]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks when a new chart cycle actually takes effect on its effective date. What do you tell her?
options: At 0901Z on the effective date
At 0000Z, as the effective date begins
At midnight local time where she flies
Whenever the app finishes downloading it
quiz.why: The U.S. changeover time for updated aeronautical information is 0901Z, so pilots and controllers use the same charts [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. Between cycles, NOTAMs carry the changes [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. A download or local midnight does not change the effective time.

quiz.q: Your learner is setting up the GPS before an IFR flight. What does the AIM's preflight database check have him confirm?
options: That it holds every published U.S. procedure
That the time of use is before its expiration
That the GPS maker supplied the data itself
That it was loaded within the past seven days
quiz.why: Preflight, the AIM has the pilot find the database issue date, verify the date and time of use is before the expiration, and check that the provider has not limited the waypoint or procedure [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. The data may come from the equipment maker or another FAA-approved source [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]], and a database may not hold every procedure because some are trimmed to fit storage [[29:263|IPH 6-13]]. The test is the expiration date, not how recently it was loaded.

quiz.q: Departing a nontowered airport, your learner is cleared "as filed, climb and maintain 6,000." An ODP exists for his runway. Who provides obstacle clearance on the climb?
options: ATC, because the clearance assigns an altitude
ATC, from the moment it says radar contact
Nobody, since no departure was assigned
The pilot, who may choose to fly the ODP
quiz.why: Under Part 91, with no ODP filed or cleared and no SID or DVA headings, obstacle clearance rests with the pilot [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]]. He may fly the ODP and should tell ATC [[29:39|IPH 1-23]]. Radar contact does not shift that responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

quiz.q: Your learner is on a SID with published altitude and speed restrictions. Departure says, "Turn right heading 090, climb and maintain 5,000." What happens to the SID?
options: It stays in effect; he resumes it after the vector
Only its speed restrictions are canceled
Canceled unless ATC says to expect to resume it
It is canceled only if the turn exceeds 30°
quiz.why: Vectored off a SID, the pilot considers it canceled, with its altitude and speed restrictions, unless the controller adds "expect to resume SID" [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. The speed restrictions go too, and there is no 30° rule.

quiz.q: Navigating by VOR on a Victor airway, your learner wants to descend from the MEA to the MOCA to get out of icing. When may he?
options: Anywhere on the segment, once ATC clears him
Within 22 NM of the VOR, once ATC clears him
Only after he declares an emergency to ATC
Within 40 NM of the VOR, the low service volume
quiz.why: Below the MEA down to the MOCA is allowed only with navigation signals available and, for aircraft using VOR, only within 22 NM of that VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]]; the MOCA assures VOR signal coverage only within 22 NM [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. In controlled airspace he still needs the altitude assigned [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]]. "Anywhere on the segment" ignores the 22 NM limit.

quiz.q: Level at 12,000, your learner is "cleared Pawling Two arrival." The chart shows "Expect to cross at 6000" at LOVES. What may he do?
options: Fly the lateral path and published speeds at 12,000
Descend at his discretion to cross LOVES at 6,000
Descend to 6,000 now, since the chart shows it
Descend to each segment's MEA as he reaches it
quiz.why: A STAR clearance without descent authorization is lateral only, with published speeds [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]; he keeps his last assigned altitude until cleared down [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. "Expect" altitudes are planning information, not restrictions, until ATC issues them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].

quiz.q: Your learner's IFR clearance included the departure frequency. When does he change to it after takeoff?
options: As soon as the airplane is airborne
Passing 1,000 ft AGL on runway heading
When the tower says to call departure
When he reaches the first fix on the DP
quiz.why: Pilots should not change to the departure control frequency until requested [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]]. In the IFH example flight the tower says "contact Departure" during the climb [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

quiz.q: After a handoff, your learner can't raise the new Center sector. What should he do first?
options: Squawk 7600 and fly the lost comm rule
Call Flight Service on 122.2 for a relay
Call on 121.5 and ask any facility for help
Call the controller who handed him off
quiz.why: If two-way contact cannot be made after a frequency change, the pilot should try the transferring controller for another frequency, after waiting at least a minute [[29:108|IPH 2-48]] [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1c]]. Flight Service is the later option, and 7600 is for an actual radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

quiz.q: In cruise your learner tunes a VOR whose identifier is silent, but the CDI is steady and the flag is out of view. What do you teach?
options: Use it; the flag proves the signal is valid
Use it only while ATC has him in radar contact
Don't rely on it; it may be off for maintenance
Use it, but only inside its terminal service volume
quiz.why: Removing the identification warns that the facility is officially off the air for maintenance and may be unreliable even with a signal [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. The only positive identification is the Morse code or voice ID [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]].

quiz.q: Your learner has just been assigned an RNAV STAR. What should his checklist confirm first?
options: That it is loaded by name and matches the chart
That every waypoint's latitude and longitude is right
That the CDI is set to 5 NM full scale
That ATC has his equipment suffix on file
quiz.why: RNAV procedures must be retrievable by name from the current database and conform to the chart [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]], and in flight the waypoints should be in the correct order and match the chart [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]]. The AIM does not require checking each waypoint's latitude and longitude [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: Center says, "Descend and maintain 5,000." Your learner, at 9,000, plans 300 fpm for comfort. What does the AIM expect?
options: Any rate he likes, since no rate was given to him
Exactly 1,000 fpm all the way to 5,000
300 fpm, if he reports leaving 9,000
Optimum rate to 6,000, then 500 to 1,500 fpm
quiz.why: Without "pilot's discretion" or a restriction, descend promptly at an optimum rate to 1,000 ft above the altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm, and advise ATC if unable to do at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10d]].

quiz.q: Cleared to cross Delta VOR at 10,000, then maintain 6,000, your learner hears before Delta, "Turn right heading 180 for vectors, maintain 6,000." Does the crossing restriction still apply?
options: Yes, until he passes the VOR
No; it was left out of the new clearance
Yes, unless ATC cancels it by name later on
No; a heading cancels every altitude
quiz.why: When the altitude to maintain is restated and earlier restrictions are omitted, those restrictions are canceled; the AIM uses this exact case, where "cross Delta at 10,000" is no longer in effect [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]] [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10g]]. The restated 6,000 still stands, so a heading does not cancel the altitude.

quiz.q: Your learner is inbound on the 160° radial and must intercept the 205° radial inbound. What intercept angle does the IFH method give?
options: 45°, equal to the difference
90°, twice the difference
20°, the smallest angle allowed
30°, a standard intercept
quiz.why: Double the 45° difference between the radials, keeping the angle between 20° and 90°: 90°, for a 295° heading [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] [[23:258|IFH 9-15]].

quiz.q: Holding heading 250°, your learner's MFD shows DTK 250° and TRK 243°. What is happening?
options: The wind is drifting him left of course
He is now 7 NM left of the course line
The GPS has lost its RAIM integrity
DTK is shown in true, TRK in magnetic
quiz.why: Track is the actual path over the ground, and the angle between heading and track is the drift angle [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. A track left of the desired track with the heading on course means the wind is drifting him left, so he corrects into the wind [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. The 7° is an angle, not a distance off course.

quiz.q: Your learner loses both radios in IMC right after takeoff on a radar SID whose chart prints its own lost communications procedure. What does he fly?
options: The general AIM lost comm procedure only
Direct to the destination at the MEA
The last assigned heading until in VFR
The lost comm procedure printed on the SID
quiz.why: Radar SIDs often include nonstandard lost communication procedures, and the pilot is expected to fly the one on the chart, not necessarily the AIM's [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

final_quiz.q: The STAR chart in your learner's TPP shows a newer number than the same STAR in his GPS database. What does the AIM say?
options: Fly the database version; it is coded data
Use it if ATC has him in radar contact
Don't use the database for that procedure
Use it, but only for the lateral path
final_quiz.why: STAR currency can be read from the number in its title, and if an amended chart is published the database must not be used for that procedure [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. RNAV procedures must also conform to the chart [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Where does your learner find whether his departure runway has nonstandard takeoff minimums and an ODP?
options: The TPP takeoff minimums and (obstacle) DP section
The airport remarks in the Chart Supplement
The notes printed on the low altitude en route chart
His clearance; ATC lists one when needed
final_quiz.why: DPs and DVAs are listed by airport in the TPP's takeoff minimums and (obstacle) departure procedures section, and a "T" on IAP and DP charts points there [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]]. ATC normally assigns an ODP only when it is needed for separation [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9g]], so the clearance is not a reliable source.

final_quiz.q: Your learner is vectored off an ODP shortly after takeoff. Who now has terrain and obstacle clearance?
options: The pilot, until he reaches the MEA
ATC, because the ODP is now canceled
Both, until he rejoins the ODP route
The pilot, since ODP restrictions stand
final_quiz.why: When ATC vectors an aircraft off an ODP, or assigns an altitude below one on it, the ODP is canceled and ATC assumes terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. ATC cannot amend an ODP's restrictions while he flies it [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h9]], but a vector ends the ODP.

final_quiz.q: A segment of your learner's airway is charted as unusable, but his VOR shows a good needle there. What do you tell him?
options: File it; the symbol only means rough signals
File it if ATC can give him radar monitoring
File it, but fly it only above the segment's MAA
Don't file or accept navigation on that segment
final_quiz.why: Pilots should not file for, or accept a clearance that includes navigation on, any segment charted as unusable [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]]. With RNAV he may ask for point-to-point clearance between valid waypoints or fixes [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is cleared to an en route fix short of the destination, and a delay is expected. Who must give him holding instructions and an EFC?
options: ATC: full instructions unless charted, plus an EFC
The pilot picks a pattern from the en route chart
Flight Service, once the delay passes 15 minutes
Nobody; he holds on the course he arrived on
final_quiz.why: ATC must issue complete holding instructions unless the pattern is charted, an EFC and its best estimate of further delay [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]]. Only if he cannot get instructions before the fix does he hold in a standard pattern on the inbound course and ask for more [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

final_quiz.q: Under Center control, your learner wants an updated destination weather report. Where should he ask for it?
options: On the Center sector frequency he is on
On the tower frequency at his destination airport
Flight Service, through an RCO or a NAVAID
On 121.5, which every facility monitors
final_quiz.why: Center frequencies are for controlling IFR aircraft; en route weather should come from Flight Service [[33:359|AIM 5-3-1a]]. In the IFH example the pilot gets a frequency change from Center and calls Flight Service on 122.1, listening on the VORTAC frequency [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

final_quiz.q: Center says, "Contact Houston Center on 126.8 at MINDO." When does your learner switch?
options: Right away, as soon as he reads it back
At MINDO, listening here until then
When the current controller stops talking
Within two minutes of the instruction
final_quiz.why: Pilots keep a listening watch on the transferring controller's frequency until the time, fix or altitude specified [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner plans a direct route off airways at 6,000 ft using VORs. What maximum spacing between the NAVAIDs does the IPH give?
options: 40 NM apart
130 NM apart
200 NM apart
80 NM apart
final_quiz.why: For operation off established airways below 18,000 MSL, use NAVAIDs not more than 80 NM apart [[29:82|IPH 2-22]], which fits the 40 NM radius of an (L) facility [[2:66|Chart Users' Guide p 66]]. 200 NM applies to (H) facilities between 14,500 and 17,999 ft [[29:83|IPH 2-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's log shows a dual VOR check 26 days ago with 5° between the receivers. Can he fly IFR on VORs today?
options: No; the dual-check limit is only 4°
Yes, the check is within 30 days
Yes, the limit is 6° for any check
No, dual checks are no longer allowed
final_quiz.why: A dual VOR check is allowed, but the most variation permitted between the two bearings is 4° [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. 6° is the limit for airborne checks [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH example flight, which item does the pilot check after taxiing onto the runway?
options: Copy ATIS and ask for the IFR clearance
Load the STAR and brief the approach
Heading indicator agrees with the compass
Call Flight Service with the time off
final_quiz.why: On the runway the IFH pilot notes the time off and verifies the heading indicator and compass agree, the transponder is in ALT, and lights and pitot heat are on [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. ATIS and the clearance come before taxi [[23:322|IFH 10-31]].

final_quiz.q: Approach says, "Reduce speed to 120, then descend and maintain 3,000." In what order does your learner act?
options: Descend first, then slow to 120
Both at once, as quickly as he can
Either order; "then" is only advisory
Slow to 120 first, then descend
final_quiz.why: When ATC joins a speed adjustment and a descent with the word "then", the sequence gives the expected order of execution [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12e]].

final_quiz.q: Cleared "climb at pilot's discretion, maintain 9,000," your learner climbs from 5,000, levels at 7,000, then wants 6,000 for smoother air. May he descend?
options: Yes, pilot's discretion allows any altitude
No; he can't return to a vacated altitude
Yes, if he reports leaving 7,000 first
No; he had to climb straight to 9,000
final_quiz.why: Pilot's discretion lets him start when he wants, climb at any rate and level off temporarily, but once he vacates an altitude he may not return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10c]]. Leveling off at 7,000 was allowed, so he did not have to climb straight through.

final_quiz.q: On a vector to final without an approach clearance, your learner sees the CDI start to center. What should he do?
options: Turn inbound; the vector implies a clearance
Turn inbound and descend to the FAF altitude
Keep the heading; query ATC if crossing
Turn away early so he won't cross it
final_quiz.why: The pilot is not expected to turn inbound unless an approach clearance has been issued, and if crossing the final approach course is imminent without word from ATC, he queries the controller [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b]].

final_quiz.q: Two minutes after takeoff in IMC, your learner's radios fail. He was assigned 5,000 and told "expect 9,000 ten minutes after departure." The MEA is 7,000. What does he fly once the ten minutes are up?
options: 9,000, the highest of the three
7,000, the MEA, for the whole flight
5,000, his last assigned altitude
His filed altitude from the flight plan
final_quiz.why: He flies the highest of the last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and the altitude ATC said to expect [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]; an expected altitude applies from the time or fix given, so he flies 7,000, the higher of assigned and minimum, until then [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]]. The filed altitude is not one of the three.

final_quiz.q: Your learner navigates only by following the magenta line on the MFD. Which risk does the PHAK name?
options: The GPS course drifts as the database ages
The line may cross high terrain or prohibited airspace
The magenta line lags the real track by minutes
The map shows true, not magnetic, courses
final_quiz.why: A pilot whose only strategy is the magenta line can fly into geographic or regulatory disaster if the straight-line course goes through high terrain or prohibited airspace, or if the display fails [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

final_quiz.q: During an RNP 1 SID, how far off the path should your learner's cross-track error normally stay on straight legs?
options: Within 1.0 NM, the full RNP value
Within 2.0 NM, as on an RNAV 2 route
Within 5 NM, the en route CDI scale
Within 0.5 NM, half the RNP value
final_quiz.why: Cross-track error should be limited to half the RNP value, 0.5 NM for RNP 1; brief deviations up to 1.0 NM are allowed during and right after turns [[40:61|AC 90-105A C.7.4.5]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, headed for a jet job, asks what changes on a high altitude route at FL 240. Which is right?
options: Altimeter on 29.92, and IFR with a clearance
VFR-on-top is available on request
Victor airways and T-routes are used
Use a local altimeter within 100 NM
final_quiz.why: At or above 18,000 MSL the altimeter is set to 29.92 [[29:103|IPH 2-43]]. Class A runs from 18,000 MSL to FL 600 [[2:67|Chart Users' Guide p 67]] and needs IFR with a clearance before entering [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]], and VFR-on-top is not permitted there [[34:9|AIM 5-5-13]]. High charts show jet routes and Q-routes [[33:378|AIM 5-3-4]] [[33:379|AIM 5-3-4]].

takeaways: Pilot and ATC duties overlap on purpose; know exactly which part is the pilot's in each phase.
Current publications first: effective dates, 0901Z, NOTAMs and a verified database.
On departure, terrain is the pilot's job unless he flies a DP or ATC is vectoring him.
A STAR clearance is lateral only until ATC authorizes descent; "expect" means planning.
Identify every NAVAID, and change frequencies only when told, at the point given.
Comply promptly, question what looks wrong, and say "unable" early.
Intercepts: orient, double the difference within 20° to 90°, lead the turn.
The MFD shows track and drift; cross-check it, and never fly the magenta line alone.
cfi_notes: Transponder timing differs by source: the IFH (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012) says to keep the transponder on standby until takeoff clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]], while the current AIM says to select altitude reporting and enable ADS-B during taxi-out on the movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]] and to have it on as soon as practical [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]]. Teach the AIM.

MEAs on STARs: the IPH says MEAs printed on STARs are not valid unless stated in an ATC clearance or in lost comm [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]; the AIM says they are not restrictions, but pilots must remain above them unless ATC clears them lower [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. Teach the AIM, which is newer and more conservative.

Revised estimates: IPH Figure 2-68 lists a revised ETA of more than three minutes as a nonradar report [[29:105|IPH Figure 2-68]]; the AIM says more than 2 minutes, with 3 minutes only in the North Atlantic [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. Teach the AIM.

PBN SIDs and STARs: the IPH says all public RNAV SIDs and graphic ODPs are RNAV 1 [[29:49|IPH 1-33]] and that RNAV STARs are RNAV 1 or RNAV 2 [[29:124|IPH 3-12]], but the current AIM says public PBN SIDs and STARs are normally RNAV 1, RNP 1 or A-RNP, with the requirements in the PBN box [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9i]] [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1e]]. Teach learners to read the PBN box.

Old names and symbols: the IFH still describes AFSS shadow boxes, TWEB and the A/FD [[23:29|IFH 1-10]] [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]; the IPH notes the A/FD is now a section of the Chart Supplement [[29:18|IPH 1-2]]. Use the current Chart Users' Guide legend for NAVAID and communication boxes [[2:65|Chart Users' Guide p 65]]. The IPH chart figures are 2010 samples marked not for navigation; brief current charts for your area. The PTS lists the IFH and the AIM as references for this Task, but most of the DP, en route chart and STAR detail is in the IPH (FAA-H-8083-16B), so expect examiners to draw on it too.

The IFH says that when a Center controller issues a heading, a direct route or "direct when able", the controller becomes responsible for terrain and obstruction clearance, but "leaving (altitude) fly (heading) or proceed direct when able" keeps it in the flight deck until above the minimum IFR altitude [[23:61|IFH 2-10]]. Make learners listen for the condition word.

Speed assignments: the AIM's recommended minimum for reciprocating and turboprop arrivals within 20 flying miles is 150 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12d]], and the IPH calls 150 knots the usual slowest assigned [[29:132|IPH 3-20]]. A slow trainer may not make speeds that suit faster traffic, so brief "unable" as a normal, correct answer.

How it is tested: FAA-S-8081-9E Area V has the evaluator select at least one Task, and its table makes Area V required when adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor airplane certificate, but not for instructors who already hold an instrument instructor rating in another category. On renewal or reinstatement, one Area V Task is required. The objective says "by describing", so expect an oral that may sit inside a combined scenario.

The AIM is not consistent on the TPP section letter: one sentence says DPs and DVAs are listed in the takeoff minimums and (obstacle) departure procedures section, "Section L", while the following subparagraph says the "T" symbol refers users to "Section C" [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]]. Teach the section by its name and the "T" symbol, not by its letter.
gaps: No source here states a Part 91 rule that requires carrying current en route charts; the sources require the charted SID or STAR to accept those procedures [[29:46|IPH 1-30]] [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]] and a current or verified database for GPS use [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].

Climb rates, descent speeds and the slowest practical approach speed for a given trainer come from the POH/AFM, which the IPH says to review before flight [[29:120|IPH 3-8]]; the handbooks give only sample airplanes.
No source describes a specific MFD's wind or track display or its menus; the AIM says to learn the installed GPS, its manual and the AFM supplement [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
No source gives a complete IFR departure, en route and arrival checklist for light airplanes; the IFH example flight and the POH are the only checklists cited here.
No source here gives a standard way to simulate radio failure in an airplane on an IFR flight plan; this lesson keeps it to ground briefings and training devices.

ATC: once vectors begin [[29:54|IPH 1-38]] and when vectored off an ODP [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. The procedure: when its lateral path and climb are flown [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9f]].
